articles.title: PSNI: Police to reduce non-emergency mental health call-outs
articles.summary: 999 calls will be triaged and if there is any risk of harm or to life, or if a crime is involved, the police will still attend.
articles.body:
Police in Northern Ireland handle 30,000 mental health calls every year, or about 80 a day on average - but a major new policy will see a significant change in how those calls are answered.

From the start of November, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) will no longer carry out concern-for-welfare checks unless there's a risk to life or harm or a crime involved.

The public will still phone 999, but calls will be assessed and handlers may pass them onto other emergency services or health and social care staff.

While reaction to the policy has been mixed, the PSNI says it is about ensuring individuals receive care from the most appropriate professional or service.

Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson previously told a Stormont committee that the number of mental health contacts received by police had reached "unprecedented levels".

He said thousands of calls about a person potentially in danger were received by the PSNI - with just 3% of those related to crime.

The policy, Right Care Right Person, is being introduced in phases in Northern Ireland.

It has been in place among some forces in England and Wales since 2023 and means police no longer attend calls where no crime has been committed, or where there is no risk of harm or risk to life.

Instead, health, social care, or community services may attend calls for help rather than the police.

Calls to 999 will be triaged and if there is any risk of harm or to life, or if a crime is involved, the police will still attend.

However, calls that require a response like a welfare check may now fall to another part of the emergency service system as opposed to the police.

The public's approach remains the same - they are asked to phone 999 in case of emergency.

One campaigner in favour of the policy is Charles Little, the son-in-law of Michael and Marjorie Cawdery who were killed in a "frenzied attack" in their home in 2017.

Thomas Scott McEntee, who was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, was sentenced to a minimum of 10 years in prison.

Their murders prompted a review into how the PSNI and the Southern Health and Social Care Trust had "missed opportunities" to detain McEntee for mental health care in the days leading up to the attack.

Little told BBC News NI that if the Right Care Right Person policy was in place at that time it may have "saved the day".

"If you're in a mental health crisis you might find a policeman turning up extremely frightening and it might worsen the situation," he said.

"So you don't always want the police to go first, even though at the moment the police are effectively the mental health front line."

Little said people "need to be looked after properly, they need to get the right care and they need to get it from the right person".

'Health services are currently at crisis point'

There have been some concerns raised about the impact the new policy may have on Northern Ireland's health and social care sector.

Dr Ross Irvine from the Royal College of Psychiatrists in Northern Ireland said "our mental health services are currently at crisis point".

"Thirty per cent of posts across the province are sitting vacant, and that has real-world implications," he said.

"A policy which removes the safety net that the PSNI are currently providing, and transfers that onto services that are already struggling to stand still, does give us cause for concern."

George Hannah, from the NI branch of the British Association of Social Workers, said: "What we're hearing from our members is this is too quick, there aren't sufficient resources in the system to do it safely at the moment.

"Most social workers would tell you that they don't want to be with the police all the time because of the potential for escalation, but I think not knowing that you have access to additional support when it's needed will increase concerns.

"This is about making sure that the right person gets the right care, but if the care isn't available in the system, then we're just moving people around."

The mental health champion for Northern Ireland, Prof Siobhan O'Neill, said she believes that the policy is an important step forward.

"This is something that needs to happen. The police were attending calls where there really wasn't a policing issue," she said.

"I think the systems are working together really well to make sure that anyone who is in crisis and is in need will receive a response."

Funding issues remain a concern for O'Neill, who has previously called for a regional crisis intervention service for Northern Ireland.

"I'm disappointed that there hasn't been the investment in the health services and mental health services to ensure that there's a backfill, alternative service," she added.

The PSNI told BBC News NI it currently responds to approximately 30,000 mental health calls each year, with a "significant proportion" of these calls coming from health workers.

"The approach is about ensuring that individuals receive care from the most appropriate professional or service.

"This will help reduce avoidable delays, improve consistency in decision-making, and support safe and lawful practice across Northern Ireland."

articles.title: P&R urged to speed up review of Guernsey relocation grants
articles.summary: Forward Guernsey believes the allowance is putting pressure on rental prices.
articles.body:
Guernsey's top political committee is being urged to prioritise a review of relocation allowances amid concerns it is putting pressure on rental prices.

Policy and Resources (P&R) said in June last year the review was "on track" to be finished by the end of September 2025.

Deputy Tom Rylatt, from Forward Guernsey, said the review should "be a priority for P&R" and the delay was disappointing.

P&R President Lindsay de Sausmarez said "several stages of work on the review have been completed" and the committee was due to consider it again shortly.

She blamed the delay on how busy the committee had been recently including delivering reforms to the island's tax system and a budget for 2027 .

A recent report from the Scutiny Management Committee linked the relocation allowances to the current high price of renting a home in Guernsey.

The current policy entitles people relocating to Guernsey for jobs with the States of Guernsey to a £5,000 grant (£6,600 for Alderney) alongside help with rental costs for up to four years, storage costs and, in some cases, support with an unsold home's mortgage.

In the last decade rents have risen by 65% to on average £2,138 per month, according to the States of Guernsey .

A freedom of information request earlier this year revealed more than £5m was spent by the States on relocation packages in 2025, the most since the support was introduced.

Deputy Rylatt said: "It is disappointing that the review has still not been completed, having originally been due in September 2025.

"With housing costs continuing to place enormous pressure on islanders, it needs to be a priority for P&R that we understand the impact these packages may be having, particularly on the rental market.

"I hope the committee will now bring this work to a conclusion and set out what changes, if any, it intends to make."

Those buying a home in Guernsey can also qualify for a £8,750 house purchase grant, while short-term recruits could receive smaller payments towards travel and moving costs.

Scrutiny Management Committee President Andy Sloan said the current policy was "excessive" and believes "such a subsidy is likely to have an upward impact on local market rents".

In June 2025 P&R said the review of these grants would look at different options for relocation support, including possible alternatives, using workforce data and financial analysis.

It said any changes would need to balance potential savings against the need to recruit and retain staff in essential public services such as health, education, social care and law enforcement.

Officials said the review was unlikely to be made public as it was looking at an internal policy but any changes would be clearly communicated by P&R.

articles.title: 1886: A New Hampshire family had an architect build 8-year-old Fanny a log playhouse with a working stove; it still welcomes visitors
articles.summary: Explore the fascinating history of Fanny Glessner's log cabin playhouse in New Hampshire, built in 1886, featuring a working stove and child-sized furnishings. This unique playhouse continues to welcome visitors today, showcasing the childhood of a future pioneer of forensic science.
articles.body: Rich families on both sides of the Atlantic gave their kids something much better long before backyard trampolines and plastic play tents. They constructed tiny versions of actual homes. Throughout the late nineteenth century, playhouses proliferated on rural estates, and most were never meant to be simple toys. A youngster might exercise the adult skills of cooking, hosting, and managing a home on these small stages.One of the finest survivors is in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. Around 1886, a log cabin playhouse was built for eight-year-old Fanny Glessner at the family’s vacation estate, The Rocks, near Bethlehem, according to the Society of Architectural Historians. It included child-sized furnishings and a working cooker, and it still stands today, open to guests. It was created by Isaac Scott and used by Fanny to practise her homemaking talents, hosting tea parties and making jams and jellies.A summer cottage in the hillsTo understand why a girl in 1886 had a cabin like this, it helps begin by looking at her family’s summer traditions. Fanny’s father, John Jacob Glessner, was a Chicago businessman who later helped found International Harvester, according to the Forest Society. The family first came to the North Country of New Hampshire in 1878 because the mountain air helped her brother George’s hay fever. After a few summers in a big resort hotel, they bought land of their own. In September 1882 they bought their first 100 acres, and a year later their home, called simply the Big House, was finished. That mansion was planned by the same family friend, Isaac Scott, who would go on to create much of the estate. His buildings included a carriage barn, a gardener’s cottage, an observatory, various summer houses and a bee house for Fanny’s mother, Frances.Playhouses of the eraFanny's cottage was hardly the only theatre of the times. Playhouses and Privilege, a new book, examines children’s playhouses built on British and American estates from the 1850s to the mid-1930s. The story begins near the start of that saga, at Osborne, at the Swiss Cottage erected in 1853 for Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. A children's cottage on the grounds of Cornelius Vanderbilt's Newport house was erected in 1886, the same year as Fanny's. In Chicago, the Sears family also built a log cabin on Prairie Avenue in the 1880s, and it survives today in Kenilworth, Illinois.Fanny’s cabin was well used. The Forest Society now maintains it for The Rocks and recalls that she spent many hours there playing, baking and making jellies. It used to be atop the hill, close by the Big House. Fanny moved it down behind the cottage later. In 1999 the Forest Society moved it again to its present place, where it is open to tourists.From playhouse to miniaturesThe cabin’s most famous resident moved on to a career that, weirdly enough, was also about establishing little worlds. Fanny grew up to become Frances Glessner Lee, who is known today as a pioneer of forensic science. After coming into the family fortune in the 1930s, she turned to forensic science in her fifties. In the 1940s, she produced the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, a series of highly realistic, miniature crime scenes to instruct homicide investigators, which the Smithsonian American Art Museum describes as a meeting point of craft and forensic science. In 2017, the museum showed all 19 studies thought to survive together for the first time at its Renwick Gallery.Fanny never really left The Rocks. Later she made the Gardener’s Cottage her home and in 1938 enlarged her cottage at The Rocks so that she could live there all year round. In 1940, she had a tea house and pond built in the gardens that had been laid out with the help of the firm of Frederick Law Olmsted. Meanwhile, her tiny crime scenes were constructed between 1943 and 1948, and for each she worked from case records and witness accounts based on actual investigations. No one knows if it was a log cabin in the forests of New Hampshire that gave her the idea. But a childhood spent maintaining a little residence, with its own cooker and sparse furniture, sits well with an adult existence of carefully crafted smaller spaces.Today, the playhouse sits on land that still functions as a Christmas tree farm. In 1978, two of the Glessners’ grandchildren donated The Rocks, by then around 1,400 acres with 22 buildings, to the Forest Society, with the proviso that there must always be a crop growing in the field. For decades, that crop has been Christmas trees. If you are planning to visit Bethlehem, you can view the cabin where an eight-year-old once baked and canned jellies, but you might want to verify the Forest Society’s guest information before you go.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event
articles.summary: Home Office cancels Andreas Malm’s planned travel to the UK, saying his presence ‘not conducive to the public good’.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – A pro-Palestine academic who was planning to travel to the United Kingdom has been denied entry because the government says his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good”.

The UK Home Office cancelled Swedish national Andreas Malm’s Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) on Wednesday, an email seen by Al Jazeera shows.

The decision came a week before Malm was due to appear on a panel organised by the British socialist magazine Tribune in London. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action – which the UK has proscribed as a “terrorist” group – is also due to appear on the panel, which will be chaired by Hala Hanina of Palestine Deep Dive.

Malm, a climate activist and author who lectures at Lund University in Sweden, told Al Jazeera that he believes his ETA was cancelled because he was due to appear on the panel. He has contacted the Home Office for an explanation but is yet to receive a response.

“I have been going regularly to the UK for decades. My position on Palestine has always been public,” Malm said, adding that his latest visit to the country was in May.

“I haven’t said anything in public about Palestine during these intervening months or written anything about it. The only thing that could have caused this [latest UK decision] is that I was due to be on a panel on Wednesday evening, where I would talk to Huda Ammori of Palestine Action,” he said.

Malm used an ETA during his May visit to the UK, which allowed him to travel to the country again later in the year without seeking reauthorisation. He said he had received no indication from the Home Office that his ETA was at risk of being cancelled before receiving an email on Wednesday confirming that it had been revoked.

In its email, the Home Office told Malm that if he wishes to visit the UK, he needs to apply for a visa, after which the office will “consider your circumstances in more detail” before making a decision. However, the government website states that the processing time for a standard visitor visa is three weeks, meaning Malm would not receive it in time for next week’s panel even if his application were approved.

Travellers from countries whose nationals do not require a visa to visit the UK generally need an ETA. These include countries in Europe, the United States and Canada, among others.

The Home Office said it does not comment on individual cases.

“Decisions to refuse or cancel an ETA on the grounds that presence in the UK may not be conducive to public good are based solely on an assessment of the potential risk an individual may pose to UK society,” it said in a statement to Al Jazeera.

The cancellation of Malm’s ETA comes amid a wider crackdown on pro-Palestine activists by the UK government, something that began under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

Tribune editor Oliver Eagleton said, “Andy Burnham’s government continues the authoritarian overreach we saw under Starmer. In this new dystopian Britain, it is now commonplace for authors and academics to be treated as terrorists because they support Palestinians facing genocide and the rights of people protesting that genocide.”

Starmer, a former human rights lawyer, was prime minister when the government proscribed Palestine Action last year.

The move classified the campaign group as a “terrorist” organisation under UK law, placing it on the same legal list as groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). The proscription has been condemned by rights groups, including Amnesty International.

Most recently, Irish novelist Sally Rooney’s books were withdrawn from sale in the UK this month due to her public support for Palestine Action.

Rooney described Malm as a “brilliant and influential” intellectual.

“For the UK government to deny him entry to Britain is not only an outrageous attack on a respected climate expert, but a sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm,” she said.

Malm’s books include How to Blow Up a Pipeline: Learning to Fight in a World on Fire and The Destruction of Palestine Is the Destruction of the Earth.

Since Palestine Action was banned, more than 3,850 people have been arrested for publicly backing the group, in largely peaceful protests.

“This is a drift towards authoritarianism that didn’t begin with me and it’s not going to end with me either,” Malm told Al Jazeera. “If I’m now being deemed a threat to the public good because I’m supposed to have a conversation with someone from Palestine Action, this is guilt by association. Where does it stop?”

Gareth Dale, reader in political economy at Brunel University of London, told Al Jazeera that the Home Office’s decision suggests the UK government intends to continue suppressing free speech under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

“Andreas Malm is one of the world’s foremost campaigners on the two defining issues of our times – climate breakdown and the genocide in Palestine. Barring him from entry to the UK represents a monstrous attempt by the Burnham government to suppress free speech,” Dale said.

“Typical of bureaucratic tyranny, no reason was given for the ban; it is cynical and Kafkaesque. As Malm has committed no crime, we are left guessing as to the motives. Burnham cultivated the impression that his government would be turning a new leaf, but instead it is replicating Starmer-era authoritarianism.”

articles.title: Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
articles.summary: Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha were charged over an incident in 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.
articles.body:
A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.

The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.

Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.

Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.

This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.

Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.

They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.

The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (£541:$723).

In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.

"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.

The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".

Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.

"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.

"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."

The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.

The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.

They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.

Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".

Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.

Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.

The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

articles.title: Smoke from wildfires killed 3,500 people in Indonesia in September: Report
articles.summary: Persistent wildfires sparked by drought have enveloped the region in smog.
articles.body:
Toxic smoke from wildfires killed 3,560 people in Indonesia last month, according to a new report.

The study, released by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) on Thursday, found that air pollution-related deaths in Indonesia surged by 42 percent in September, rising from an estimated 3,740 people killed in August to 5,310.

Toxic smoke from forest and land fires caused 3,560 deaths last month, the report said. “Chronic, non-fire emissions from urban and industrial air pollution sources” caused another 1,750 deaths, the Helsinki-based think tank found.

Toxic fire smoke accounted for 94-99 percent of air pollution-related deaths in Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, and more than 80 percent on Sumatra, the regions worst affected by the fires, the report notes.

Deaths on the southern island of Java, meanwhile, remained largely tied to urban and industrial sources, the study found.

It added that the number of citizens exposed to “unhealthy” to “hazardous” air quality reached a record peak of 58 million in September.

“Citizens inhaling hazardous-level air in Kalimantan alone nearly tripled from 2.8 million to 6.4 million during the worst days of the month,” it found.

Amid an El Nino weather pattern, Indonesia has been dealing with devastating wildfires sparked by severe drought, which have led to deforestation and sent toxic smog across the Southeast Asian archipelago.

It has also raised pollution levels in neighbouring countries, including Malaysia , Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor.

The government in Jakarta is facing increasing criticism for its response to the fires. On Wednesday, it defended its approach, noting it has deployed more than 72,000 people to carry out cloud-seeding and firefighting operations, activated more than 2,100 doctors and health workers in hard-hit areas, and distributed 5.3 million masks.

articles.title: Brittany Mahomes helped raise over $200,000 for food allergy charity in 2023, now a project she launched with Patrick has its first approved Kansas City restaurant, with trained staff and strict kitchen rules
articles.summary: Brittany Mahomes has spent years turning her family’s personal experience with food allergies into practical support for other families, and that work is
articles.body: Brittany Mahomes has spent years turning her family’s personal experience with food allergies into practical support for other families, and that work is now producing a visible change in Kansas City restaurants. In 2023, she helped launch a GivingTuesday fundraising match campaign with FARE, the Food Allergy Research and Education organization, raising more than $200,000 for food allergy programs. The following year, she and Patrick Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies Foundation formalised its commitment by partnering with FARE to create 15 and FARE, an initiative designed to make dining out, community food access, and everyday life safer for people living with food allergies. That initiative has now reached an important milestone. Joe’s KC has become the first Kansas City area restaurant recognised under the 15 and FARE program, with all of its locations receiving the designation, according to KCTV5. Customers can look for a “15 and FARE approved” sign at the restaurant, a signal that staff have completed extensive training and that the kitchen follows specific procedures to reduce the risk of accidental allergen exposure. For families who often approach restaurant menus with anxiety, the recognition represents more than a plaque on a door. It is an attempt to make a routine meal feel safer and more predictable. Read on for more details about it here:A personal mission becomes public actionThe Mahomes family’s involvement is deeply personal. Brittany and Patrick Mahomes have two children with severe peanut allergies, and Brittany has spoken openly about the constant vigilance that food allergy families carry with them. In materials shared by FARE, she described food allergy as a life threatening disease that requires constant attention, noting that it affects 33 million Americans, including her own family. Her experience as a parent navigating emergency room visits, daily precautions, and the fear of an unexpected reaction has become central to the public face of the initiative.That personal connection helped fuel earlier charitable work. During GivingTuesday in 2023, Brittany Mahomes and OWYN, a brand known for protein shakes free of the top nine allergens, launched a fundraising match campaign for FARE. The campaign raised more than $200,000, and FARE later honoured Brittany with its FARE Champion Award at the 15 and the Mahomies Foundation Gala in Kansas City. FARE CEO Sung Poblete said at the time that Brittany’s willingness to share her family’s story had inspired thousands of food allergy patients and their families to keep fighting.The partnership announced in November 2024 took that fundraising momentum and turned it into a structured community program. 15 and FARE brings FARE Neighborhoods and FARE’s Food Allergy Academy training to the Kansas City area. The goal is not simply to raise awareness, but to equip restaurants, food banks, pantries, school staff, and community health workers with the knowledge and systems needed to respond appropriately when someone has a food allergy.What 15 and FARE requires from restaurantsBecoming a 15 and FARE Restaurant Partner is not a symbolic endorsement. According to FARE, participating restaurants must train 90 percent or more of their food service staff, conduct monthly on site audits for three consecutive months, create a written food allergy management policy if they do not already have one, and demonstrate allergen transparency on their menus. Recognition is valid for one year, which means restaurants must maintain their standards rather than treat approval as a one time achievement.The program is free for restaurants in Kansas City, Kansas, and Kansas City, Missouri. FARE provides training and resources to businesses of all sizes, removing a major barrier for smaller restaurants that may want to improve allergen safety but lack the internal expertise or budget to build a program from scratch. Families dining out are encouraged to look for the “15 and FARE Restaurant Partner” logo as an indication that the business has met the program’s requirements.At Joe’s KC, the impact of the training was immediate. Front of house manager Lane Dougherty told KCTV5 that the process was an eye opener, particularly in showing how even a tiny amount of an allergen can affect a person. The restaurant’s allergen list has expanded to two pages, identifying which menu items contain which allergens and flagging ingredients produced in facilities that handle allergens. The list covers wheat, gluten, milk, dairy, peanuts, tree nuts, egg, soy, shellfish, MSG, and sesame.Strict kitchen rules behind the recognitionThe practical changes at Joe’s KC illustrate why formal training matters. When a customer mentions an allergen, the request is passed to a staff member at the front counter, who communicates with the sandwich maker or kitchen team. That employee then changes gloves and cutting boards before preparing the order. The restaurant also uses separate fryers, keeping breaded items on one side and gluten free items on the other. These are small operational details, but they can make the difference between a safe meal and a dangerous exposure.The restaurant’s experience also shows how hidden allergens can appear in familiar dishes. KCTV5 reported that Joe’s KC barbecue beans contain Worcestershire sauce, which includes shellfish and soy. That kind of detail is easy for a customer to miss and difficult to identify without clear staff training and transparent menu information. Dougherty said more customers are now asking questions, and staff are able to provide useful answers rather than uncertainty.For Brittany Mahomes, that shift in everyday restaurant culture appears to be the point. When the 15 and FARE partnership was announced, she said the goal was to ensure Kansas City families have access to the resources they need to manage food allergies confidently and safely. She emphasised that the work is not only about awareness, but about being ready to act. Patrick Mahomes added that food allergy reactions can happen at any time and in any place, and that families should not have to face those struggles alone.A broader effort for Kansas CityJoe’s KC may be the first recognised restaurant, but it is unlikely to be the last. The 15 and FARE initiative is part of FARE’s larger Neighborhoods effort, which was created to reduce inequities in access to care, support, and resources for people with food allergies in marginalised communities. In other areas where the initiative has operated, FARE reported a 25 percent increase in families visiting an allergist and a 38 percent increase in epinephrine prescriptions, alongside improved confidence among food allergic individuals in managing their condition.Kansas City is the seventh FARE Neighborhood, and the local rollout includes training for community food banks and pantries as well as restaurants. FARE and 15 and the Mahomies have also hosted public education events, including a 2026 back to school event featuring an allergen free lunch demonstration, expert panel discussions, health screenings, and family activities. The initiative also includes access to FARE’s free online course, “Save a Life: Recognising and Responding to Anaphylaxis.”The first approved restaurant gives the program a concrete example of what success can look like. It shows that allergen safety can be built into daily kitchen routines, staff communication, menu transparency, and customer service. More importantly, it offers families in Kansas City something they often struggle to find: a clearer sense of where they can eat with greater confidence.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has finally explained the controversy surrounding his reported $12,000 restaurant bill in Japan.
articles.body: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has finally explained the controversy surrounding his reported $12,000 restaurant bill in Japan. After facing criticism online, Lacy admitted that a language barrier made him believe he had to pay the entire amount, even though he later learned he only had to cover the extra food that had already been prepared. He also admitted that he joked about the situation during his livestream instead of correcting his earlier comments. Lacy has now apologised to the restaurant for the unwanted attention it received.Lacy reveals why he thought he owed $12,000 at Japan restaurantIn a post on X on October 29, Lacy explained that he initially misunderstood what the restaurant staff told him because of the language barrier. articles.title: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
articles.summary: Was Spain’s second major train collision this year caused by human error or failures in its once touted high-speed rail network?
articles.body: BARCELONA, Spain — Was Spain’s second major train collision this year caused by human error or failures in its once touted high-speed rail network? It depends on whom you ask. Spain’s transport minister was quick to lay most of the blame on a traffic controller’s poor judgment for Wednesday’s collision in Toledo province, which killed 69 people. But railway unions are pushing back. They point instead to what they describe as deteriorated working conditions — fewer traffic controllers with more work than ever — that have made it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of 45 million passengers annually. A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly crash, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged to get to the bottom of it. “This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened,” Spain’s King Felipe VI said on Thursday after visiting injured passengers in a Toledo hospital. “We will have to take measures so this never happens again.” The timeline of the catastrophe given by the government The chain of events that ended in disaster started at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, when the communication system key to the functioning of the line’s security system went down. The system, called LZB, monitors the position of trains and can even trigger the automatic braking of a train to prevent a collision. That malfunction meant that human controllers based at a control post in Madrid took over full responsibility for monitoring the positions and safety of the trains on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) between Madrid and Seville. At that time authorities believe there were six trains on the affected stretch of track. At 8:36, a controller told one train, belonging to the state-owned RENFE company, that it could start running again at normal speed. The other train, operated by privately owned IRYO, located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) down the line, also tried to restart, but the engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and informed the controller. At 8:53 the collision occurred, derailing carriages and shredding parts of the trains to bits. It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, further south, one train jumped the track and hit another train going the other direction, killing 46 people. What the minister says Transport Minister Óscar Puente, who is under pressure to resign, called the controller’s decision to let one train restart at full speed while the other remained still “inexplicable” and “erroneous.” Puente said that the RENFE train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a stop signal active on that line. “An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision,” Puente told reporters. The decision “was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light,” he said. What the unions say Unions, however, argue that the context matters. Raquel Ayllón, spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that the workload is regularly too much for the current staff to safely handle. She said that traffic controllers have been asking for more personnel for years, while the safety systems keep failing. “We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” she said. “Human error isn’t incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.” Spain’s union for train engineers, SEMAF, said that this was not the first time the three-decade-old LZB security system, which is still in use on the Madrid-Seville line while being phased out, has gone offline and left human operators to fend for themselves. “The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago,” said Diego Martín, spokesperson of the SEMAF union of Spain’s train engineers. “It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past.” Train workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand the government fulfill its commitments to improve safety conditions after the January crash. Representatives from several unions also criticized what they called the “irresponsible” leak of audio clips of conversations between the control room and the train engineers to Spanish media. Could privatization have overloaded the rail system? Spain’s railways only service state-owned trains until it opened its high-speed rail to private operators in 2021. Both of this year’s collisions involved a train operated by RENFE and one operated by IRYO. Rail traffic increased after the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for instance, the average number of daily trips increased from 56 to 89 between 2019 and 2024, according to the SCF union. A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on railways. “We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

articles.title: 'Will be game over for America': Elon Musk raises three 'concerns' against Democrats ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk backed Republicans on Friday and warned that a Democratic sweep of the US House of Representatives, Senate and
articles.body: Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk backed Republicans on Friday and warned that a Democratic sweep of the US House of Representatives, Senate and presidency in 2028 could lead to what he described as the “end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word”, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.In a series of posts on X on Thursday, Musk outlined three changes he fears Democrats could pursue if they gain control of the White House and both chambers of Congress: granting statehood to Washington DC and Puerto Rico, legalising people living in the US illegally, and expanding the Supreme Court.“My biggest concern is that if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028, they will,” Musk wrote, before listing the three possibilities as:1. Make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate. 2. Open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority.3. Increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority.He then added: “It would be game over for America.”Musk argued that the changes would allow Democrats to consolidate their political power and turn the US into a “permanent one-party state”. He called on voters to ensure Republicans retain at least 51 Senate seats in 2029, saying: “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.”His remarks come just days before the US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers, but Democrats are seeking to regain control amid voter concerns over inflation, the economy and the administration's policiesThe billionaire's warning comes amid a broader political battle over the balance of power in Washington. Statehood proposals for Washington DC and Puerto Rico, immigration policy and the possibility of expanding the Supreme Court have been subjects of political debate, with significant disagreement between the two parties.Musk's millions for RepublicansMusk has emerged as one of the biggest financial backers of Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections. The Washington Post reported on October 23 that he had contributed about $446 million to influence the election cycle, largely through Republican-aligned political action committees.His contributions include substantial funding for the Senate Leadership Fund, which supports Republican Senate candidates, and America PAC, his own political action committee. He has also backed efforts to help Republicans retain control of the House.The spending marks a renewed push by Musk to influence US politics after his public falling-out with Trump last year.Why are the 2026 midterm elections crucial?The November 3 elections will determine which party controls the House and Senate for the final two years of Trump's presidency. A change in control could significantly affect the administration's legislative agenda, spending negotiations and congressional oversight.Republicans hold a narrow majority in the House and a 53-47 advantage in the Senate. Democrats need net gains in both chambers to take control.Recent polling has favoured Democrats in the race for the House, while the Senate contest remains more uncertain. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted through October 26 put Democrats ahead of Republicans by 53% to 44% among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot. A CBS News/YouGov poll also projected Democrats on course for 229 House seats, although Republicans retained a narrow path to holding the chamber.The elections are being fought against a backdrop of concern about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. A recent AP-NORC poll found that about 80% of voters identified the economy or cost of living as a major election issue.Even if Democrats win one or both chambers, their ability to enact major legislation would remain constrained by Trump's veto power and other institutional checks. articles.title: CHRIS JOHNSON: The data center boom is rescuing forgotten American towns
articles.summary: From Ellendale, North Dakota, to Loudoun County, Virginia, data centers are transforming communities with billions in tax revenue and lower property taxes.
articles.body: With the midterm elections approaching, data centers have become an increasingly popular political target. Politicians are raising alarms about their impact on communities, with some calling for construction moratoriums or outright bans. There's been plenty of fearmongering. But the more Americans learn about data centers, and the more communities experience their benefits firsthand, the stronger the case for continued development becomes. Data centers have existed for decades, but the rapid growth of artificial intelligence has dramatically increased the demand for computing power. Americans understandably have questions about what this development means for electricity prices, water supplies, and their quality of life. Newer facilities are increasingly being designed with technologies that can address these concerns, including closed-loop cooling systems and quieter operations. DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS Yet much of the national debate overlooks what data centers are already delivering to communities across America. Take Ellendale, North Dakota, a town of 1,100 people. Before Applied Digital's new $11 billion data center development, the town collected roughly $400,000 annually in sales taxes. In the first seven months of 2026 alone, that figure jumped to $3.5 million. THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS That revenue is helping the city repave its roads and renovate its senior center. A historic opera house is being restored. For a small town, this kind of investment can transform the community for generations. And Ellendale is far from alone. Schools across America are seeing enormous benefits from the data center boom. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's massive investment has helped fund an increase in annual teacher bonuses ranging from $10,000 to $50,000. Think about what that means for a working family. Teachers who have dedicated their careers to educating children are receiving a life-changing financial benefit, while the school district becomes an attractive destination for talented educators. It's hard to imagine a politician campaigning against higher teacher pay or better schools. Yet those are precisely the kinds of benefits communities stand to lose when development gets blocked. PROPOSAL WOULD PAY HOMEOWNERS 'DATA CENTER DIVIDENDS' TO COUNTER GROWING BACKLASH The benefits extend to homeowners struggling with the rising cost of living. In Loudoun County, Virginia, data centers generate 45% of county revenue. That enormous tax base has allowed local officials to cut homeowner property tax rates every year for a decade. TO BEAT CHINA IN AI, AMERICA MUST WORK WITH COMMUNITIES — NOT AROUND THEM In neighboring Henrico County, local leaders used data center revenue to fund a $60 million Affordable Housing Trust Fund, helping young families and first-time buyers purchase homes. At a time when housing affordability is dominating political conversations, building data centers is helping some communities make the American Dream a little easier to achieve. Electricity prices are another major concern, and understandably so. Families are already struggling with higher utility bills, and the arrival of a major new industrial customer can raise legitimate questions about who pays for new infrastructure. But the enormous, predictable electricity demand from data centers also creates opportunities to finance new generation and grid investments, spreading infrastructure costs across a larger customer base. In Georgia, agreements involving new large electricity customers, including OpenAI, are projected to lower residential power bills by $180 annually by 2029. With the right arrangements in place, the arrival of data centers can mean lower costs for the families already living in these communities. And the benefits extend well beyond tax revenue and household expenses. Trade unions have been among the most vocal supporters of data centers because of the good-paying jobs they create. Building these facilities requires years of work for skilled tradesmen, with new projects creating opportunities for the next generation of American workers. In Baltimore, Maryland, IBEW Local 24 expanded its membership by 50% alongside data center construction. In Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, IBEW Local 163 doubled its ranks following construction of an Amazon data center. Politicians have spent decades promising to bring back good-paying blue-collar jobs. Here is an industry creating enormous demand for exactly those workers. Of course, developers have a responsibility to work with residents and local governments to address legitimate concerns. Communities deserve clear answers about electricity costs and water use. They should also understand how the investments taking place in their backyards will benefit local families. But when data centers are developed responsibly, the economic benefits can be enormous. Communities are rebuilding roads and improving schools. Homeowners are seeing lower tax burdens, and skilled workers are finding new opportunities. For decades, politicians have campaigned on championing the Forgotten Man and bringing economic opportunity back to communities that have struggled to attract investment. Now, data centers are delivering billions of dollars in private investment to many of those very places. We're watching a new industrial boom take shape across America, creating jobs and revitalizing communities that Washington has spent decades promising to help. Before politicians rush to stop it, they ought to take a serious look at what those communities are gaining. articles.title: Psychology says children who repeatedly forget to brush their teeth or get dressed after being asked may still be developing the ability to remember future tasks, and research explains why visual cues can help
articles.summary: Getting children ready in the morning can sometimes feel like a test of patience. You ask them to brush their teeth, get dressed and comb their hair.
articles.body: Getting children ready in the morning can sometimes feel like a test of patience. You ask them to brush their teeth, get dressed and comb their hair. They say they will do it, but a few minutes later, you find them playing with a toy or doing something completely different. So you repeat the instructions, only to find yourself reminding them again.Before assuming that a child is being careless or deliberately ignoring you, it is worth understanding how memory develops during early childhood. Psychologists explain that remembering to complete a task later is a skill children are still learning. Knowing what they have to do does not always mean they can remember to do it at the right time. This ability is called prospective memory. It helps us remember future intentions, from taking something to school to completing a routine before leaving the house. For young children, managing these small responsibilities can be surprisingly challenging.Knowing what to do is not the same as remembering to do itImagine asking a four-year-old to brush their teeth after breakfast. The child may understand the instruction and even repeat it correctly. However, once breakfast is over, a toy, a conversation or another activity may capture their attention. The original instruction can slip from their mind. This happens because prospective memory involves more than remembering information. Children must recognise when a task needs to be done, notice the right cues and shift their attention away from whatever they are doing.Research published in Cognitive Development has examined how this ability develops in preschoolers. Findings suggest that children's performance improves as they grow, but remembering an intention and acting on it at the correct moment remain two different challenges. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology looked at 88 children between three and six years old. Researchers examined whether verbal reminders helped children remember to carry out an intended action. The reminders did not significantly improve their performance.The findings do not suggest that parents should stop communicating with their children. Instead, they highlight why repeating the same instruction may not always solve the problem. A child who is busy with another activity may need something more noticeable than another verbal reminder.Make the next step easier for children to noticeSometimes, the solution may lie in changing the surroundings rather than repeating instructions. When children can see the things they need, it may become easier for them to remember the next step in their routine. Parents can try keeping the toothbrush in an easy-to-reach place, setting out clothes before bedtime or placing the schoolbag near the door. A chart with simple pictures showing the morning routine can also help children understand what comes next.A 2023 review published in Psychological Research explored strategies that may improve children's prospective memory. It considered visual and verbal cues, among other approaches, and found that visual reminders could support children's ability to remember intended actions. However, the results differed depending on the task and situation.This means a picture chart or a strategically placed object may be worth trying, but parents should not expect it to work immediately or in every situation. It is also important to consider what the child is doing when a request is made. Asking them to get dressed while they are concentrating on a game or another activity can make it harder to switch tasks. Allowing them to finish what they are doing before introducing the next step may help reduce distractions.When children are not forgetting, but putting things offThere is another reason a child may leave a task unfinished. They might remember exactly what they need to do but simply prefer doing something else. This behaviour is known as procrastination. It involves delaying an intended task even when there is a reason to complete it. Research published in Developmental Psychology in 2023 examined procrastination among children aged three to six. Based on parents' reports, younger children often delayed everyday routines and cleaning up, while older children were also reported to put off chores and schoolwork. The research explored how procrastination relates to developing abilities such as executive functioning and thinking about the future. These skills help children manage their actions, stay focused and work towards a goal.For parents, making routine activities more enjoyable may be one way to encourage cooperation. Brushing teeth can become a short game, while getting dressed can turn into a race against a favourite song. Giving children a choice between two outfits or allowing them to complete a small task independently can also make them feel more involved. The idea is not to turn every responsibility into a reward-based activity. Rather, making an otherwise dull task more interesting may help children approach it with greater enthusiasm.Help children practise thinking aheadChildren also need opportunities to understand why certain tasks must be completed before something else happens. Parents can encourage this by asking simple questions about situations they may face later. Before leaving home, for example, ask, “What might you need if it gets cold?” Instead of packing everything for a child, parents can ask what should go into the schoolbag. Such conversations encourage children to think about what may happen next and prepare for it.A study published in Child Development in 2020 examined how children aged three and four use past experiences when thinking about future situations. It found that children at this age can have difficulty using what they already know to anticipate what they might need later. Parents can make these conversations more engaging by using familiar people or imaginary characters. Asking what a friend might wear on a rainy day or what a superhero would pack for a school trip can encourage children to consider another person's needs and think ahead.The next time your child forgets to brush their teeth or delays getting dressed, remember that these tasks involve skills that are still developing. Repeated instructions may not always be enough, but visible cues, manageable routines and playful activities can offer useful support. Children do not become organised overnight. With practice, guidance and patience, they gradually learn to remember their responsibilities and complete them more independently.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican, was among those who called for its withdrawal. The controversy also raised concerns among Republicans that it could affect other candidates on the party's ticket, including Senate candidate Jon Husted, who said he would not have advertised.However, President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance defended Ramaswamy and the campaign's decision to use the footage. Trump described the criticism as "very unfair" and defended the advertisement in a social media post."Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt,’" Trump wrote.Ramaswamy entered the Ohio governor's race in February 2025 and secured Trump's endorsement. His campaign has centred on economic growth, tax reductions and changes to the state's education system.He has proposed eliminating Ohio's state income tax, lowering property taxes and raising academic standards in public schools.Ramaswamy won the Republican primary in May 2026 and will face Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, in the general election.You use AI every day. articles.title: What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza?
articles.summary: More than 25 dockworkers’ trade unions in 110 ports of 22 countries are going on strike on October 30.
articles.body:
Dock and port workers have long had a tradition of solidarity with the oppressed, upheld by strong labour unions and workers’ rights.

In February 2025, nearly a year and a half into Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza , dockworkers’ unions from Mediterranean countries came together to disrupt weapons shipments to Israel and Western countries’ military support of the onslaught.

“Weapons need transport, infrastructure, and workers’ hands to reach their destination,” Markos Bekris, leader of Greece’s dockworkers’ union, ENEDEP, at the Port of Piraeus in Athens, told Al Jazeera. “That is where our power lies.”

Now, dock and port workers in 22 countries across five continents are holding a strike on Friday, which workers and researchers told Al Jazeera is expected to be “historic” in scale. The International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers – also called “Dockworkers do not work for war” – involves 110 ports and 25 trade unions.

“Every union will do what they choose, but be connected to the same principles and struggle,” Francesco Staccioli, the national secretary of transport and ports in Italy’s USB trade union, told Al Jazeera.

The unions’ main demand is “an immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and all imperialist wars”.

Mohammed al-Attar, a dockworker who left Gaza in 2015 and is now based in Hamburg, Germany, said the workers “are the power”.

“We can save thousands of lives if we stop working just for two days,” he said.

Al-Attar feels hopeful about the global strike, but is “deeply disappointed” in his trade union Ver.di in Germany, which he accused of “incomprehensible silence” over Gaza .

What is the International Day of Action of Dockworkers and Port Workers?

In early 2025, dockworkers in the Mediterranean area came together to discuss how to concretely act “against privatisation, and against the genocide in Palestine”.

The original meeting included five unions organising in 20 ports across five countries, but continued to grow. The unions met several times, first in Athens, then in Genoa, and later in Istanbul. That was where unions from more than 35 ports published the Istanbul Declaration in May this year, and declared October 30 as their day of action.

In a statement, the unions called for the “recognition of an independent Palestinian state, recognised by the international community, within the 1967 borders and with East Jerusalem as its capital”, and “an end to the US-Israeli wars of aggression in the Middle East and against Iran, and full solidarity with the peoples of Cuba, Venezuela and Sudan”.

“Refusing the war is giving humanity a chance to live better. This is what I’m really convinced about,” the USB’s Staccioli told Al Jazeera.

How many ports and unions are taking part?

More than 25 dockworkers’ trade unions, representing more than 110 ports in 22 countries and regions across five continents, are taking part. Most of the strikes will happen at regular working hours, but in France, Italy, India, Greece and Turkiye, 24-hour strikes have been called.

Strikes of up to two hours have also been announced in Morocco, Cyprus and other ports.

Organisers told Al Jazeera that workers and trade unions from other sectors have been called on to join with port workers, notably in Greece, while in Italy the USB has called for a general strike.

“It’s bigger than we thought,” Staccioli said. “This has spread all over the world.”

No Harbour for Genocide (NHG), a campaigning collective that researches weapon supply chains, supports the action. A spokesperson told Al Jazeera that maritime infrastructure was important in “facilitating military trade within the context of the genocide in Palestine”.

Dockworker unions in India, Sweden, Denmark, Australia, Brazil, Mexico, Uruguay and the west coast of the United States have all pledged to take part, the spokesperson added.

The Palestinian labour movement endorsed the strike and called on more to join, urging unions to “escalate Boycott, Divest, Sanctions (BDS) pressure to end all state, corporate and institutional complicity in Israel’s illegal occupation, apartheid and genocide.”

Of the ports participating, Genoa, Livorno and Gioia Tauro in Italy, Marseille in France, Piraeus in Greece, and Tangier in Morocco all have proven links to weapons shipments to Israel, according to No Harbour for Genocide.

The group said that between August 2025 and September 2026 it tracked 315 shipments of components for Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, moving through 56 commercial ports in 29 countries. All these 56 ports are expected to be on strike on October 30 , representing a major disruption, even if only for a day.

NHG said it expects that more than $2bn worth of cargo will sit idle on October 30 .

“Up to 95 percent of Israel’s imports and exports travel by sea, relying on port infrastructure across the Mediterranean, ” the campaign’s spokesperson said. “Tangier, Piraeus, Gioia Tauro and Genoa, where the largest vessels unload containers onto smaller ships for the rest of the sea, are a few of the Mediterranean’s most frequently used transshipment hubs. All four are taking part on Friday.”

“The participating Mediterranean ports handle 63 percent of all container activity in the sea,” the spokesperson added, noting that “between southern France and Piraeus, the striking ports hold 74 percent of container activity. Worldwide, the ports taking part [in the strike] handle 13.5 percent of global shipping.”

Linda Maggiore, an Italian journalist and activist, said that she has discovered several examples of increasing weapons shipments from Italy’s major ports to Israel since the start of the war on Gaza.

“In Europe, a regulation on military mobility is about to be approved, which will make it even easier for arms to be transferred without scrutiny,” Maggiore told Al Jazeera. “Blockades are essential actions, because they make it clear that civil society does not wish to be complicit.”

From the Vietnam war to Iraq, the USB’s Staccioli said that “dockworkers have a long tradition of rallying against any imperialist war or aggression in the world.”

In Greece , union leader Bekris is facing prosecution for a protest in which he and other workers blocked the loading of a container holding 21 tonnes of ammunition destined for Israel in October 2024.

“We carry forward the tradition of workers who refuse to load weapons against other people,” Bekris told Al Jazeera on the eve of the global strike. “Our hands get covered in grease and sweat every day. We refuse to let them be stained with the blood of other people.”

articles.title: Uttarakhand's Joshimath: Rescue operations on after Indian helicopter crashes in Himalayan state
articles.summary: The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
articles.body:
A search for survivors is under way after a helicopter carrying six people, including five pilgrims, crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.

Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter had crashed near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district. Rescue teams have been dispatched to the mountainous area, but the condition of those on board remains unclear.

The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.

The cause of the crash is also not yet known. The incident happened amid reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.

Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.

Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.

Helicopter services have become increasingly popular among pilgrims seeking to avoid difficult mountain journeys, but their safety has come under scrutiny following a series of accidents.

Friday's incident happened amid heavy rain in the region. India's weather department had issued an orange alert for the area, warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds.

Dhami said a joint rescue operation was under way involving the district administration, disaster management department and State Disaster Response Force.

"I am continuously monitoring the entire incident," he added.

Dhami also said he had ordered that anyone seriously injured be airlifted for treatment.

In June 2025 , seven people were killed when a helicopter carrying pilgrims crashed near Kedarnath. Another seven died in a crash on the same pilgrimage route in October 2022.

Several other helicopter accidents were reported during the 2025 pilgrimage season, prompting aviation authorities to tighten safety checks and restrict some operations.

articles.title: On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote
articles.summary: Border issues helped propel Trump in the Rio Grande Valley in 2024. His deportation policies could bury Republicans.
articles.body:
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Leaning over plates of tamales, pan dulce, and sugar skulls, community organisers and local residents in the border city of Brownsville remembered the dead.

This year’s Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, vigil honoured victims of state violence, including those killed in immigration enforcement and detention. Just days before the US midterm election on November 3, the event reverberated in a region long subject to Washington, DC’s shifting political winds.

“The atmosphere here in the Rio Grande Valley when it comes to ICE detentions and the ICE raids, there’s just the overall feeling amongst folks that there’s no real due process to this,” said Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser.

“What is it that we can do to move together and build together to try to make it past this, and make that change that we seek?”

Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border and immigration policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia raised her hand to ask advice on how to find a lawyer able to navigate the aggressively shifting policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has used both an increase in physical enforcement, as well as a reinterpretation of administrative policies, to fuel its mass deportation campaign.

Garcia’s aunt, a well-known member of the community in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks ago, after being called to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) hearing. There she learned she had missed a court date related to her immigration status.

In the stress of the moment, she signed a voluntary deportation form.

“Within 36 hours, she was deported,” Garcia told Al Jazeera, tucked between bookshelves. “People are waking up, and they’re remembering that politics, regardless of what branch you’re in, it’s going to impact you every day.”

Views on immigration are complex in the Rio Grande Valley, a geographic and cultural region located in subtropical southeast Texas with about 1.5 million residents. That complexity has only increased in recent years as border policy and immigration enforcement have become increasingly partisan, leading, reformers say, to dramatic policy swings that prevent more sustainable solutions.

It is not difficult to find Latino – or Tejano, the local term for Texans of Latino descent – residents wary of the years preceding Trump’s return to office. After the restrictive policies of Trump’s first term, border crossings increased dramatically under US President Joe Biden, fuelled in part by the end of a COVID-era policy that made asylum seekers wait for their cases to be processed in Mexico.

Some felt the border region was left to deal with the fallout from the influx. That discontent has been credited, in part, with Trump’s success in the once-reliably Democratic region in the 2024 presidential election.

In Hidalgo County, home to the city of McAllen, Trump won 51 percent of the vote in 2024, a three-point margin over Kamala Harris. In 2020, Biden beat Trump in the county by 17 percentage points.

In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five percentage points in 2024, despite a 13-point loss in 2020.

Voter Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old resident of Brownsville, assessed the two years since Trump took office as a “positive change”, with fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases to be processed.

Upon taking office, Trump declared a state of emergency at the border, staunching asylum claims in what rights groups say runs counter to US law. The US Supreme Court has since ruled that US border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil to claim asylum.

“A lot of people claim that they support illegals and want to let them in,” said Arizpe, a regular Republican voter, “but then, I say ‘well let them in your house’. And they don’t want to do it, right?”

On border policy, “at first, I supported Trump,” said Martin Torres, a 55-year-old who cast his ballot for Democrats at a public library in Brownsville as part of the state’s early voting.

But domestic enforcement, and its impact on the local workforce, soured his views.

A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.

Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Rights groups say the decision effectively allows racial profiling.

In Texas, a state law also lets local officials stop individuals they suspect entered the country illegally.

“I just see a lot of discrimination going on,” said George Castorena, a 46-year-old department of education worker, who said he was voting for change.

To be sure, midterm elections can only offer incremental change on an issue as entrenched as immigration enforcement and border policy.

Democratic control of the House of Representatives would at best serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration legislating more immigration enforcement funding and policy, while opening the door to investigations into the administration’s approach.

Control of the Senate, which could be determined by the contest between Texas Republican Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico, could further increase the party’s leverage.

A change in the governor’s office, meanwhile, could end Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s myriad uses of state agencies to support federal immigration enforcement. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa, if she were to pull off an upset, would be largely constrained by a likely Republican-dominated state legislature and a mountain of pre-existing law.

Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.

A poll conducted by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas found that only 34 percent of respondents from the area felt that immigration enforcement by both local and state officials had made their communities safer. Fifty-three percent said it made their lives harder without improving safety.

Meanwhile, 64 percent felt ICE tactics have gone too far. The numbers broadly align with polls showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores in two Rio Grande Valley congressional districts.

Republicans, eyeing Trump’s success in 2024, viewed the races as strong prospects early in the election season.

“What this survey conveys is: people along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024,” Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at ACLU of Texas, told Al Jazeera.

Even prominent community figures who support Trump’s policies acknowledge a broader change in sentiment.

Eli Lara, the lead pastor at the non-denominational New Life Family Church in McAllen, Texas, said locals have been dismayed by the wide scope with which the administration has targeted undocumented individuals.

“The immigration issue is bigger because [the community] is seeing people being taken,” he told Al Jazeera. “I don’t like the separation of families, but here’s the thing: there are consequences for choices.”

That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.

“He’s been faithful [to the church] for two, three years, but they picked him up,” Lara said. “Why? Because he had a bad criminal record in the past. God forgives, but the government doesn’t.”

Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.

She pointed to several instances that have recently shaken the region, including the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in the town of Alamo in the Rio Grande Valley, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July 2026 in the Texas city of Houston.

“I’ve had a lot of people tell me, ‘Why do I care about politics? Politics doesn’t affect me,'” she said. “And with all of these ICE raids, they realise politics does affect them, and it sucks that it took a lot of trauma to really bring that to people.”

articles.title: Villa Guardamangia, Queen Elizabeth II’s former Malta home, is being restored seven years after the government bought it, but the royal museum is still closed
articles.summary: Villa Guardamangia, Queen Elizabeth II’s former Malta home in Pietà, is undergoing a multimillion-euro restoration led by Heritage Malta, the national
articles.body: Villa Guardamangia, Queen Elizabeth II’s former Malta home in Pietà, is undergoing a multimillion-euro restoration led by Heritage Malta, the national heritage agency, seven years after the government bought the residence. Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip lived there as newlyweds between 1949 and 1951, while he was stationed with the Royal Navy. The house remains closed to visitors as conservators work to return it to its mid-twentieth-century appearance. The project is expected to cost just over €12 million and take around three years to complete. No reopening date has been confirmed, so the planned museum has yet to welcome visitors.How the Maltese government bought Villa Guardamangia after heritage groups urged it to step inThen Prime Minister Joseph Muscat told parliament in October 2019 that the government had bought the villa, saying it could become a major tourist attraction, Times of Malta reported. He did not reveal the price, although the property had been advertised at €6.5 million. Heritage organisations including Flimkien Għal Ambjent Aħjar, Heritage Malta and Din L-Art Ħelwa had long argued that the neglected building needed saving. Muscat added that talks would begin with the Pietà Council on how to handle the visitors the site was expected to draw. The villa was formally entrusted to Heritage Malta in June 2020, according to the agency.Restoration work at Villa Guardamangia is under way and has already secured the crumbling façadeThe works were signalled a year before they began. Minister for National Heritage Owen Bonnici said at a press conference held at the villa in October 2024 that Heritage Malta would issue the first tenders, TVM News reported. By 1 October 2025, restoration and conservation were under way. Ruben Abela, an architect with Heritage Malta, told TVM News that parts of the façade at risk of collapse had been stabilised and other sections reinforced. Garden statues and household furnishings left to deteriorate for years have been conserved, and painted decorations on the walls have been uncovered so they can be restored. European sources are covering €10 million of the bill.Why Princess Elizabeth remembered Malta as her happiest time and a chance to live a normal lifeThe late Queen regarded the time she spent living at the villa as the happiest of her life, Times of Malta reported, and it remains the only place outside Britain she called home. Lady Pamela Hicks, one of her bridesmaids and a cousin of Prince Philip, told the Daily Mail that Princess Elizabeth loved the island because she could wander through town and shop, living as any other naval officer’s wife did, according to Nine. Royal commentator Victoria Arbiter told the podcast The Windsors that it was the only time the couple were free simply to be newlyweds. The Queen was driven past the villa during a visit in 1992 and was given a painting of it in 2015. On seeing it that year, Nine reported, she is said to have remarked that it looked rather sad.Heritage Malta says the aim is to open the villa as a historic house representing how the royal family used it.
