articles.title: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.summary: ROME — Tens of thousands of people were getting ready to take to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
articles.body: ROME — Tens of thousands of people were getting ready to take to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending. After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe, more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest. The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France, where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security. Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels. In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later. Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.” The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.” Major demonstrations were also expected in 50 other cities and towns across Italy, while protesters are also expected to blockade ports in Genoa, Livorno, Trieste and elsewhere. It comes after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month. Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest. Protesters also stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month. But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting. “There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation. The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.

articles.title: Aid convoy enters besieged Ukrainian town Oleshky
articles.summary: Moscow and Kyiv have so far observed the six-day truce as evacuations from Oleshky get under way.
articles.body:
An ‌aid convoy has entered the Russian-held town of Oleshky, in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, after weeks of efforts to organise a relief operation ⁠for residents.

The Russian newspaper Izvestia said on Friday that the aid convoy carried food ⁠and medical supplies as the six-day United States-brokered localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into its third day. However, Moscow stressed that the truce in Oleshky could not be linked to a broader ceasefire.

Ukraine Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Russian ⁠counterpart Yana Lantratova met in Oleshky overnight, Russian state TV channel Vesti reported.

Lantratova said 25 buses with at least 750 seats stood ready to evacuate those seeking to leave the city, which was seized by Russian forces soon after Moscow’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Evacuations will continue until 2pm local time (12:00 GMT).

Lubinets said in a statement that remaining residents would be able ⁠to leave ⁠safely ⁠and underscored the importance of maintaining the ‌six-day US-brokered ceasefire.

Russia and Ukraine on Thursday announced that demining operations had been completed around Oleshky and that the operation to deliver aid to residents and let a number of them leave was ready to begin. Lantratova added that two people were ⁠killed in the demining effort in the city.

The White House insists that US First Lady Melania Trump mediated the ceasefire in Oleshky, which she said was “on the brink of disaster”, with food and medical supplies running perilously low for the up to 2,000 people still there.

She began talks after hearing about the humanitarian situation in the city at one of her events during the United Nations General Assembly session in September, the White House said. Once home to about 24,000 people, Oleshky has no electricity, heat or running water as it approaches another harsh winter.

But the Vatican has offered its own narrative, suggesting that the pope was responsible for helping the pause in fighting through phone calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated city since Tuesday but remain otherwise locked in the war that began more than four years ago.

The situation ⁠in Oleshky is an ‌isolated case that should not be extrapolated to the broader ⁠peaceful settlement process ⁠in Ukraine, Kremlin spokesman ⁠Dmitry Peskov said ⁠on ⁠Friday on Russian state TV.

Russia struck an industrial facility near Kremenchuk ⁠while hitting the Ukrainian capital and Kharkiv, the second ⁠biggest city, Ukrainian officials said on the Telegram messaging app.

Moscow said it hit energy infrastructure in and around Kyiv, as well as in the Dnipropetrovsk region, port facilities in the Odesa region and cargo vessels it said were ‌used ‌by the military.

The Russian capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said on Telegram that Russian authorities downed most of the more than 850 drones headed overnight towards Moscow.

articles.title: Seoul crush scene to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
articles.summary: Bereaved families say they were appalled to see footage of the Itaewon disaster included in Modern Warfare 4.
articles.body:
Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty game after an angry reaction from victims' families.

Real life news coverage of the 2022 disaster which killed almost 160 people was included in an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4 to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.

Bereaved families said they were "appalled" to see the footage - which included people being removed on stretchers, body bags on the street and resuscitation efforts - repurposed for the game.

Activision, which makes Call of Duty, has since apologised and confirmed it would be removed in the game's next update on 12 November.

The crush happened in the narrow alleys of Seoul's Itaewon district when more than 100,000 people went to the area to celebrate Halloween four years ago.

The streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.

In a statement on Thursday , the families of those who died said the disaster "was a tragedy that caused hundreds of casualties, and citizens who took part in the rescue or witnessed it have suffered from trauma until now".

"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used to create a scene in a game.

"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless."

Activision confirmed it had used real news coverage of the disaster "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insisted it had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".

Confirming on Friday that the footage would be removed in a statement, the company offered its condolences and apologised to the bereaved families and victims who have been hurt by this incident.

The decision was welcomed by the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association, however the group told the BBC they had not received a direct apology from Activision.

Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.

Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.

At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told BBC Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".

articles.title: Melania Trump-brokered evacuation begins in Ukraine amid fears over escape route
articles.summary: An evacuation mission was underway in a Russian-occupied city in Ukraine, during a truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump and with Pope Leo XIV’s involvement.
articles.body: A landmark evacuation and humanitarian aid mission was underway Friday inside a devastated Russian-occupied city in Ukraine, during a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo XIV. Ukrainian officials have described the operation in Oleshky as one of the most significant pauses in fighting since Russia launched its full-scale invasion more than four and a half years ago. Humanitarian teams from both sides were on the ground early Friday, with the first lady posting to X that they were “delivering aid and preparing the convoy for civilian evacuation.” However, any sense that the ceasefire might yield wider progress in the war was tempered by Russian missile strikes on other cities ahead of what is predicted to be a bitter winter for Ukraine. Some Ukrainians in the city were also worried about where they would end up after being evacuated. Though Oleshky is just across the Dnieper River from Ukrainian-held Kherson, the planned escape route to Ukrainian-controlled territory runs through Russia and its ally Belarus. Some residents told Sky News they feared they would not be allowed to continue into Ukraine, leaving them weighing whether to board the buses or remain in the devastated city. Designated routes into the city had been cleared of mines. A convoy of 25 buses with a total capacity of 750 passengers, along with nine ambulances and more than 50 medical professionals, had been prepared to help residents leave, according to Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova. “People who wish to leave for the territory of the Russian federation are gathering here,” Lantratova said in a video from the city posted Friday. “Over there are also people who wish to leave for the territory of Ukraine. Everyone will be given the opportunity to do so. People are gradually boarding the buses.” Ukrainian representatives also said they were on the ground. “We are in Oleshky!” Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said in a statement, adding that the ceasefire had now lasted more than 80 hours. “I am now speaking with local residents on the ground to hear about their needs and to understand what help they need most.” Kyrylo Budanov, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office, said in a statement that it was “an important operation, and it must be continued. For Ukraine, the life of every citizen matters. We keep working.” Russian forces seized Oleshky in the early stages of the 2022 invasion and fighting has devastated the city since. The dominance of drone warfare in this conflict makes aboveground travel extremely dangerous, and services and supplies have deteriorated sharply since May. Oleshky’s pre-invasion population of more than 20,000 has dwindled to an estimated 2,000, with those left behind surviving on tiny amounts of grain and edible weeds. This perilous situation caught the attention of Leo, who called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16 to express his “deep concern” and urge a pause in fighting to allow evacuations and aid deliveries. The first lady’s office said she learned of the city’s plight during a United Nations gathering in September and used contacts developed through her efforts to reunite Ukrainian children with their families to help broker the truce. Both sides have praised her contribution. The ceasefire was announced Oct. 23 and took effect Tuesday. It is due to expire at 10:59 p.m. Sunday, Kyiv time (3:59 p.m. ET). Asked if the truce could be used as a blueprint for ceasefires in other locations, Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists Monday that “for humanitarian purposes — it absolutely could.” That was “especially given the direct, highly positive, and coordinating involvement of the American side — American negotiators and U.S. first lady Melania Trump — in this process,” he added. “We greatly value these efforts, and, certainly, this could set a precedent.” Outside this relative pocket of calm, however, the war ground on. Ukraine’s air force said Russian strikes had hit 17 locations overnight, while its air defenses had shot down or suppressed 96 drones and three missiles. Meanwhile, drone manufacturer Fire Point said Ukraine had used its FP-1 drones to strike the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia’s Samara region. Ukrainian officials have not commented.

articles.title: Arkansas officials took just 1.62 acres from a family trust's land and initially valued the loss at $417,825; after an 11-year fight over road access, an appeals court upheld a $3 million jury award
articles.summary: A dispute over a small strip of land in Conway, Arkansas, grew into a decade-long legal battle after a highway project restricted access to the remaining
articles.body: A dispute over a small strip of land in Conway, Arkansas, grew into a decade-long legal battle after a highway project restricted access to the remaining property. The Arkansas Court of Appeals has upheld a jury's $3 million compensation award, rejecting the state's arguments that the verdict was excessive and that evidence about replacement roads should not have been admitted.A government acquisition involving just 1.62 acres of land has resulted in a multimillion-dollar compensation dispute in Arkansas, highlighting how a small taking can affect the value and potential use of a much larger property. In a ruling delivered on October 28, 2026, the Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld a $3 million jury verdict awarded to the William Major Lewis Trust after a highway project restricted the property's direct access to Dave Ward Drive in Conway. The decision in Arkansas State Highway Commission v. Lewis, published by Justia, affirmed the trial court's judgment despite the commission's challenge to the award and the evidence considered by the jury.The dispute began on August 7, 2015, when the Arkansas State Highway Commission condemned portions of two adjoining tracts belonging to the trust, whose co-trustees are William Lewis and Cody Lewis. The land was acquired for a road project involving the widening of Dave Ward Drive, also known as Highway 286, and the construction of roundabouts near its intersections.The commission initially deposited $417,825 with the court as its estimate of just compensation. But the trust argued that the impact went beyond the land physically acquired. By restricting direct, unrestricted frontage access to Dave Ward Drive, the project affected how the remaining property could be accessed and commercially developed.The dispute was about more than the land takenBefore the acquisition, the trust and its tenant had used direct access points along Dave Ward Drive to reach the property. After the project, the owners were left with alternative access routes, including an unimproved road on the eastern side and access through the old Amity Road on the western side of one tract. The commission maintained that access to both tracts remained available. The property owners, however, argued that the remaining routes did not provide commercially equivalent access to land fronting a major road.That distinction became central to the case. The affected property was near Interstate 40, and its frontage along Dave Ward Drive was important to its potential commercial use. According to the court's account, the trust said it could not develop the land as intended without building replacement roads. Cody Lewis testified that the City of Conway required the owners to construct a relocated Amity Road and an east-west connector road before they could make commercial use of the property adjoining Dave Ward Drive. The trust said it spent approximately $4 million to $4.5 million on the roads and had to use seven acres of its remaining property for their construction.The commission disputed the connection between those expenses and the taking. It argued that the owners would have needed to undertake road construction to develop the property even if the highway project had not occurred.Two very different valuationsThe gap between the two sides' estimates was substantial. The commission's appraiser valued the total compensation at $417,825, using comparable property sales without including a separate calculation for damage to the remaining land. The trust's appraiser, Diana Thompson, estimated just compensation at approximately $3.8869 million. Her assessment used comparable sales and, for one tract, an income-capitalisation approach that accounted for lost rental income after the tenant relocated.Cody Lewis also gave testimony about the property's market value before and after the acquisition. He said the loss of access and the need for additional roads reduced its commercial potential. The case proceeded to a jury trial in June 2024. The jury awarded the trust $3 million, an amount lower than its appraiser's estimate but substantially higher than the commission's valuation.The trial court subsequently awarded interest on the compensation balance, along with attorney's fees, costs and appraiser's fees. The commission appealed, challenging the admission of evidence about road-building costs, the sufficiency of the evidence supporting the verdict and the award of legal expenses.Why the appeals court upheld the awardThe Court of Appeals rejected the commission's arguments. It said evidence about the cost of restoring access can be considered when determining how a partial taking affects the market value of the remaining property. Such costs cannot automatically become the measure of compensation, but they can help a jury assess the difference in value before and after the acquisition. The jury had been instructed that road-restoration costs could be considered only as an aid in determining just compensation, not as the damages figure itself. The appeals court said the $3 million verdict fell within the range of valuations presented at trial and found no basis to overturn it.The court also upheld the related award of attorney's fees, costs and expenses. Under the relevant Arkansas law, such fees may be awarded when a jury's compensation figure exceeds the amount deposited by the commission by more than 20%. The threshold was met in this case. The ruling does not mean the trust was awarded the full amount it claimed for road construction. Rather, the court found that the jury could consider the evidence when assessing the property's loss in value.A dissent raises concerns over taxpayers' moneyThe decision was not unanimous. Judge Brandon J. Harrison dissented, arguing that the road-building evidence should not have been admitted in the way it was. He questioned whether the owners would have had to build similar roads to develop the property regardless of the highway acquisition.The dissent also highlighted the scale of the proposed road network and raised concerns about making taxpayers bear development costs that might otherwise have fallen on the landowners. It pointed to testimony suggesting that some road construction would have been necessary even without the condemnation.The majority, however, concluded that the jury had heard competing evidence and was entitled to decide whether the access restrictions caused the claimed reduction in value.You use AI every day. articles.title: Evacuations begin in occupied Ukrainian town as Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire holds
articles.summary: Hundreds of people from an occupied town in southern Ukraine who survived months without basic supplies are set to be evacuated on Friday under a ceasefire agreement negotiated by first lady Melania Trump.
articles.body: Hundreds of people from an occupied town in southern Ukraine who survived months without basic supplies are set to be evacuated on Friday under a ceasefire agreement negotiated by first lady Melania Trump. The town of Oleshky in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson has been under continuous Russian occupation since April 2022. Some 2,000 people, including 50 children, have been stuck in the badly destroyed municipality, Ukrainian authorities say. All access routes were either heavily mined or swarming with drones, making an escape impossible. The humanitarian situation has deteriorated in recent months. The town was reported by Ukrainian authorities to have ran out of food and other supplies in September, with no access to electricity, gas, medicine, and other essentials. The dire situation has raised alarm around the world, with international organizations, faith leaders and others calling for urgent action. Residents have been reportedly resorting to searching for scraps and eating weeds, with bodies of people who died left in the streets. The temporary truce went into effect on Tuesday and has since expanded across the Kherson region. The ceasefire has also brought relief to Kherson, the Ukraine-controlled capital of the region, which has been under near constant drone attacks from Russia. It is set to expire on Sunday. Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets traveled to Oleshky to personally escort the evacuees into Ukraine-controlled territory – becoming the first high-profile Ukrainian official to openly travel to occupied areas under Russian control and Russia since the start of the war. “We are in Oleshky,” he said in a statement. “People who want to go to the territory of the Russian Federation are gathering here, and there are people who want to leave for the territory of Ukraine. Everyone will be provided with such an opportunity.” Lubinets’ Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, was also present in Oleshky and the two were seen in videos standing next to each other while talking to local residents. The evacuation is scheduled to begin in early afternoon local time. According to Lubinets, 25 buses with the capacity of 750 seats are part of the operation. They are expected to travel through Crimea, Russia and Belarus and arrive to the Ukrainian border at some point on Saturday. Videos shared by Lubinets’ office show the ombudsman greeting groups of emotional residents in Oleshky, discussing their journey. In one, he is seen talking to people leaving about those who want to stay, telling them, “I was told that it’s their own choice. We will at least make sure that at least some humanitarian aid comes.” Some 40% of the town’s prewar population of around 24,000 managed to flee to Ukraine-controlled territories when it was still possible early in the war, according to the Institute for the Study of War, a US-based conflict observer. Thousands of others have escaped since then, but many remained, either unable or unwilling to leave. The town plays an important part in Russia’s military operations in the region. It sits near the banks of the Dnipro river, directly opposite Ukrainian positions. As the two sides fire at each other, the people in Oleshky are caught in the middle. All escape routes towards Ukraine gradually disappeared as the Russian occupation intensified. And while it had previously been possible to flee the city by going deeper into Russia-controlled territory, this has also become impossible in recent months, as fighting intensified and all routes out were either mined or swarming with drones. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Russia of mining the access routes to the town in an effort to stop people from leaving.

articles.title: Police probe Jeffrey Epstein’s time spent at Balmoral with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor
articles.summary: Scottish police are investigating the time convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein spent with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor at Balmoral, a private royal estate in Scotland which is a favored retreat for the monarchy.
articles.body: Scottish police are investigating the time convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein spent with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor at Balmoral, a private royal estate in Scotland which is a favored retreat for the monarchy. “We have received information and active enquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage,” a Police Scotland spokesperson told CNN on Friday, without giving details about the investigation. “All enquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those enquiries,” the police spokesperson said. “We would never confirm details of ongoing enquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.” British newspaper The Daily Express reported that the investigation was related to allegations women were “trafficked” to Balmoral. Since the release of the Epstein files, Mountbatten-Windsor, known as Prince Andrew until his brother King Charles III stripped him of his titles, has faced a slew of allegations over his links to the late sex offender. He was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office in February and interviewed under caution before being released. The scandal has left Mountbatten-Windsor’s already battered reputation in tatters and plunged Britain’s royal family into crisis. Pictures previously released by US prosecutors in 2021 appear to show Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, the financier’s right-hand woman currently serving time in a US federal prison for sex trafficking and other crimes, at Balmoral in 1999. Buckingham Palace has consistently said that it does not speak for Mountbatten-Windsor and does not comment on active police investigations. Mountbatten-Windsor has vehemently denied any and all wrongdoing in his dealings with Epstein. Police have said their investigation into misconduct in public office, relating to his time as a trade envoy for Britain, is still ongoing.

articles.title: Original Hertfordshire Traitors star became film actor after show
articles.summary: First series traitor Kieran Tompsett appears in the latest He-Man film.
articles.body:
A contestant from the first UK series of The Traitors has said the show transformed his life and helped launch his acting career.

Kieran Tompsett, 46, from Stevenage, Hertfordshire, was recruited as a traitor towards the end of the 2022 series, he was banished during the final episode, but memorably hinted at the identity of the last remaining traitor as he left.

Tompsett said the experience prompted him to ask: "What else do I want to do now?" He then decided to attend Ashley Walters' Kingdom Drama School.

He said: "I've trained for a year and a half and I've done three or four films now, I've done some supporting artist work to get some experience on set."

Earlier this year he appeared in the He-Man film Masters of the Universe, and will appear in an upcoming dark comedy called Damaged Goods.

Tompsett was working as a solutions consultant when he appeared on the hit BBC show in 2022 and now runs an AI workflow automation company.

He said: "I've just secured lead cast in a horror film for next year as well, so yeah, I'm going down a completely different path."

However, the former traitor admitted he initially found being in the public eye difficult.

He said: "I think in the first two years it was overwhelming. Anyone who has been on it will know you can't even go to Tesco and buy a meal deal at lunchtime without everyone staring at you.

"It's not a negative thing, but your privacy goes... I've always stopped and talked to everyone, still, it's quite hard to experience that loss of privacy, really."

articles.title: Qatari officials in Iran in bid to revive ceasefire deal with US
articles.summary: The mediation mission comes amid speculation about a potential resumption of hostilities.
articles.body:
Qatari mediators have arrived in Tehran in an apparent bid to negotiate a revival of a ceasefire in the conflict between the United States and Iran.

A Qatari delegation, in coordination with US officials and headed by the senior adviser to the Gulf nation’s Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, arrived in the Iranian capital on Friday morning for talks and consultations, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported.

This latest diplomatic push comes amid conflicting signals from Washington. A letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei, delivered on Sunday, has reportedly been well received.

However, US President Donald Trump has warned Gulf allies to prepare themselves for a brief high-intensity military campaign after next week’s US midterm elections , according to The Wall Street Journal.

A Qatari delegation delivered the letter from Vance, which reportedly proposed a new diplomatic process to Iran in a bid to stave off a new round of US strikes.

The newspaper quoted an informed source as saying the letter and follow-up discussions did not cover specific peace terms, but rather a potential “framework for negotiations”.

Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, said that while there was no official reaction from Tehran, sources said the tone of the letter was much more respectful than previous correspondence from the US administration, which was welcomed by Iranian authorities.

Serdar said the Qatari delegation was thought to have travelled to receive Iran’s response, and to elaborate on a potential new diplomatic path.

Sources told Al Jazeera that a meeting could possibly be held within a week, either in Doha or Istanbul.

articles.body: CHENNAI: Suburban commuters in Chennai will get extended train services to Tiruvallur, Kadambattur and Sullurupeta, along with a new midday service from Tiruvallur to Moore Market Complex, as Southern Railway’s revised suburban timetable is set to come into effect on Nov 1. The changes include additional stoppages, revised fast and slow local services, and new timings on key routes. The revised schedule will come into effect for Sunday services on Nov 1 and weekday services on Nov 2.On the Chennai Central–Arakkonam section, Train No. 43230 will leave Tiruvallur at 12.25pm and reach Moore Market Complex at 1.45pm. An existing morning service from Moore Market Complex to Pattabiram will be extended to Tiruvallur as Train No. 43209, leaving at 7.10am and arriving at 8.30am. Its corresponding service will start from Tiruvallur at 8.45am and reach Moore Market Complex at 10.20am.Two other services will be extended to Kadambattur. Train No. 43903 will leave Moore Market Complex at 2pm and reach Kadambattur at 3.25pm, while Train No. 43904 will leave Kadambattur at 3.35pm and reach Moore Market Complex at 5.05pm. Two evening services to Arakkonam will swap their stopping patterns. The 7.30pm fast local will become a slow local, stopping at all stations, while the 7.45pm slow local will become a fast local.On the Chennai Central–Sullurupeta section, a morning service will be extended from Gummidipundi to Sullurupeta, leaving Moore Market Complex at 5.20am and reaching Sullurupeta at 7.55am. The return service will leave Sullurupeta at 8.10am and reach Moore Market Complex at 10.40am.On the Chennai Beach–Chengalpet section, Train No. 40904 from Arakkonam will get an additional stoppage at Guduvancheri at 9.20am.MRTS timings between Chennai Beach, Velachery and St Thomas Mount will remain unchanged.Passengers can check revised timings and stoppages on the NTES app.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news.
